title: October Night Sky Brings Hidden Jupiter and Meteor Showers
summary:
October’s longer nights give skywatchers several events to look for, NASA notes. Among them are a planetary disappearing act and two meteor showers.

Before sunrise on October 6, people in parts of eastern and central North America could see Jupiter slip behind the Moon’s thin crescent for about an hour. Astronomers call this a lunar occultation—when the Moon blocks a more distant object. The event was visible without a telescope, though binoculars helped. Timing varied by location; in some places it happened around 4 a.m. Eastern time.

The Draconid meteor shower peaked on the evening of October 8 into early October 9. Unlike many showers that are best after midnight, the Draconids can be watched soon after nightfall, around 9 p.m. Eastern. They appear to come from the constellation Draco, the dragon. The display is usually modest—only a handful of meteors per hour—but this year’s dark skies near new Moon helped. The best views come away from city lights after eyes adjust to the dark.

Another shower, the Orionids, peaks around October 21. Those meteors are bits of debris from Halley’s Comet. When Earth passes through the trail, the particles burn up as bright streaks. NASA estimates suburban viewers may see about 3 to 6 meteors per hour, with more under darker skies. The Orionids seem to radiate from Orion. A bright waxing gibbous Moon may hide fainter meteors until the Moon sets around 3 a.m. local time, when Orion is higher before sunrise.

No special equipment is required for these shows—just clear skies, patience, and a safe dark place to look up.
why_it_matters: Seasonal sky events invite kids to practice careful looking and connect calendar dates with real astronomy. Knowing when moonlight helps or hurts viewing makes nights outdoors more successful.

background_read: Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through trails of dusty debris left by comets.
The Moon can hide planets or stars for a short time when its path lines up just right.
Darker skies make faint meteors easier to see, while bright moonlight can wash them out.
Many sky events can be enjoyed without telescopes if you have clear weather and a safe viewing spot.
